videos.title: Le Chatelier’s Principle: Concentration and Temperature | Year 12 Chemistry
videos.description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/chemistry/year12/module5/lesson05

Predict how an equilibrium responds when a substance is added or removed, or when the mixture is heated or cooled. Use iron thiocyanate and cobalt colour changes to explain the reaction rates behind each shift, then distinguish the immediate change from the response on concentration and rate graphs. Practise a prediction with nitrogen dioxide and dinitrogen tetroxide.

0:00 The colour-change puzzle
0:56 The immediate change
1:30 The system responds
2:41 Reading the graphs
4:18 Temperature and cobalt
6:03 A heat memory aid
6:51 Practice question
7:49 Working through the answer
9:17 Key notes

Chemistry 2017: Year 12 Module 5, Equilibrium and Acid Reactions. Supports explaining and predicting concentration and temperature effects using Le Chatelier’s principle.
Syllabus dotpoint (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, Module 5):
"investigate the effects of temperature, concentration, volume and/or pressure on a system at equilibrium and explain how Le Chatelier’s principle can be used to predict such effects, for example:
- heating cobalt(II) chloride hydrate
- interaction between nitrogen dioxide and dinitrogen tetroxide
- iron(III) thiocyanate and varying concentration of ions (ACSCH095)"
"explain the overall observations about equilibrium in terms of the collision theory (ACSCH094)"
Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/chemistry-stage-6-2017

Prerequisite: Dynamic equilibrium in a closed system and how forward and reverse reaction rates approach equality. Next: How pressure, volume and catalysts affect an equilibrium.

videos.title: How Single-Celled Organisms Reproduce: Fission and Budding | Year 12 Biology
videos.description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/biology/year12/module5/lesson03

Explain why a single cell copies its DNA before dividing, then compare binary fission in bacteria and protists with budding in yeast and a budding protist. Work out how repeated doubling increases cell numbers and distinguish reproduction from bacterial conjugation, which changes cells that already exist.

0:00 How one cell becomes two
0:55 Binary fission
1:26 Repeated doubling
2:31 Budding in yeast
3:25 Fission and budding in protists
4:14 Conjugation is different
5:25 Practice question
7:19 Working through the answer
9:19 Key notes

Biology 2017: Year 12 Module 5, Heredity. Supports explaining mechanisms of reproduction in bacteria, fungi and protists through binary fission and budding.

Syllabus dotpoint (NSW Biology Stage 6, 2017, Module 5):
"explain the mechanisms of reproduction that ensure the continuity of a species, by analysing sexual and asexual methods of reproduction in a variety of organisms, including but not limited to:
- animals: advantages of external and internal fertilisation
- plants: asexual and sexual reproduction
- fungi: budding, spores
- bacteria: binary fission (ACSBL075)
- protists: binary fission, budding"
Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/biology-stage-6-2017

Prerequisite: Asexual reproduction, clones, DNA and the nucleus, and powers of two. Next: What happens after a mammal’s egg is fertilised.
